items.prompt:
Read this full class discussion:
  Teacher: 'Should animals be kept in zoos? Why or why not?'
  Ava: 'Yes, because zoos protect endangered animals.'
  Ben: 'I see Ava's point, but I think zoos are not good for animals because they are not in their natural habitat.'
  Cara: 'Building on Ben's idea — maybe the answer is in the middle. Some zoos help endangered animals; others just show them for entertainment.'

Rank the responses from best to worst discussion participation and explain why.
A) Cara > Ben > Ava — because each response builds more on previous ideas
B) Ava > Ben > Cara — because Ava spoke first
C) Ben > Cara > Ava — because Ben disagreed
items.answer: A) Cara > Ben > Ava — because each response builds more on previous ideas

steps: Ava gives a relevant, correct starting answer but does not link to others' ideas (she goes first, so this is fine).
Ben explicitly links to Ava ('I see Ava's point') and adds a counterargument with reasoning.
Cara does the most complex work: she synthesizes BOTH previous views ('maybe the answer is in the middle'), builds on Ben, and adds new nuance.
Each student's contribution is stronger because it builds more explicitly on what came before.
The order of first-speaking does not determine quality of discussion participation.

items.prompt:
A student notices that a classmate's comment seems to contradict something said earlier in the discussion. She wants to point this out respectfully. Which response is best?
A) 'Wait — that doesn't match what Noah said a minute ago. Noah, you said fish breathe underwater. But Lily just said fish come up for air. Can we figure out which is right?'
B) 'You're wrong. Noah was right.'
C) 'That is confusing. Let's just move on.'
items.answer: A) 'Wait — that doesn't match what Noah said a minute ago. Noah, you said fish breathe underwater. But Lily just said fish come up for air. Can we figure out which is right?'

steps: Option B is disrespectful — it dismisses one student without exploring the conflict.
Option C ignores the contradiction — the group misses a learning opportunity.
Option A names the contradiction, links to specific comments from both Noah and Lily, and invites the group to resolve it.
This is advanced collaborative discussion: tracking multiple contributions and asking for clarification across ideas.

items.prompt:
A discussion has gone on for several minutes. A student realizes that the group has drifted from the original question ('What is the main message of the story?') and is now talking about whether the story is funny or not. What is the best response?
A) Enjoy the funny discussion and forget the original question
B) Politely refocus: 'This is interesting, but I think we moved away from the main question — what is the main message? Can we come back to that?'
C) Raise your hand and tell the teacher someone broke the rules
items.answer: B) Politely refocus: 'This is interesting, but I think we moved away from the main question — what is the main message? Can we come back to that?'

steps: Students share responsibility for productive discussions, not just teachers.
Option A abandons the learning goal entirely.
Option C creates conflict and is not student-led refocusing.
Option B acknowledges the conversation while politely redirecting to the original topic.
This is a high-level discussion move: monitoring and steering the conversation.

items.prompt:
Read this scenario: A student consistently interrupts others, speaks for long stretches, and rarely asks questions. The group is getting frustrated. Using the discussion rules, identify TWO specific problems with this student's behavior and ONE suggestion for how to address each.
A) Problem 1: interrupting (fix: wait for others to finish); Problem 2: dominating (fix: pause and invite others to share)
B) Problem 1: using complete sentences; Problem 2: being off topic
C) Problem 1: not raising a hand; Problem 2: speaking too quietly
items.answer: A) Problem 1: interrupting (fix: wait for others to finish); Problem 2: dominating (fix: pause and invite others to share)

steps: Problem 1: Interrupting breaks the rule 'speak one at a time.' Fix: wait until the speaker finishes completely before talking.
Problem 2: Speaking for long stretches and rarely asking questions breaks the collaborative balance. Fix: pause more often and invite others ('What do you think?').
Option B describes different problems (complete sentences, off topic) that are not what this scenario describes.
Option C (hand raising, volume) are also not the main problems in this scenario.

items.prompt:
A student says: 'I want to add to the discussion, but I am not sure my idea connects perfectly. Should I stay quiet?' What advice do the discussion rules suggest?
A) Yes — only share ideas if you are certain they connect
B) No — sharing uncertain ideas and asking whether they fit ('Does this connect to what we are discussing?') is good collaborative practice
C) Yes — uncertain ideas ruin discussions
items.answer: B) No — sharing uncertain ideas and asking whether they fit ('Does this connect to what we are discussing?') is good collaborative practice

steps: Collaborative discussions thrive when students share thinking — including tentative ideas.
Asking 'Does this connect?' is a form of seeking clarification and inviting feedback.
This models intellectual humility and keeps the conversation open.
Requiring certainty before speaking would silence many valuable contributions.

items.prompt:
A class is discussing: 'What should you do if you find a lost dog?' Three students speak:
  Mira: 'Bring it to the animal shelter.'
  Theo: 'I agree with Mira. Or maybe check for a tag with the owner's phone number.'
  Sofia: 'Adding onto both — check for a tag first so you don't have to go to the shelter if you don't need to. The tag is faster.'
What is Sofia doing that Theo also did but to a lesser degree?
A) Building on multiple previous contributions and synthesizing them into a better answer
B) Disagreeing with both Mira and Theo
C) Asking for clarification
items.answer: A) Building on multiple previous contributions and synthesizing them into a better answer

steps: Theo builds on Mira ('I agree with Mira') and adds a new option.
Sofia builds on BOTH ('Adding onto both') and explains which approach is more efficient and why.
Sofia synthesizes — she takes multiple ideas and combines them into a more complete answer.
Synthesis is the highest level of building on others' talk.

items.prompt:
During a discussion, a student notices that no one has explained WHY they think what they think — everyone just stated opinions. What should she say to improve the discussion quality?
A) 'Good points everyone. Let's move on.'
B) 'Can each of us try to explain WHY we think that? Like, what's the reason behind your idea?'
C) 'I think everyone is wrong.'
items.answer: B) 'Can each of us try to explain WHY we think that? Like, what's the reason behind your idea?'

steps: Strong discussions include not just opinions but reasons and evidence.
Option A closes down the discussion without improving it.
Option C is disrespectful and unproductive.
Option B invites everyone to deepen their contributions by adding reasoning.
This is asking for further explanation — a discussion rule — applied to the whole group.

items.prompt:
A student in a discussion says: 'I want to push back on what Leo said. Leo said the main character is selfish, but I think she is actually afraid — and fear sometimes LOOKS like selfishness. Does that change anyone's thinking?' Evaluate this response across three dimensions: (1) respecting the speaker, (2) adding new reasoning, (3) inviting further discussion.
A) (1) Respects Leo by naming him; (2) offers a new interpretation (fear vs. selfishness); (3) invites others to reconsider ('Does that change anyone's thinking?') — this is high-quality collaborative discussion
B) (1) Disrespectful because she disagreed; (2) no new reasoning; (3) closed the discussion down
C) This response is not appropriate for a classroom discussion
items.answer: A) (1) Respects Leo by naming him; (2) offers a new interpretation (fear vs. selfishness); (3) invites others to reconsider ('Does that change anyone's thinking?') — this is high-quality collaborative discussion

steps: Dimension 1: Naming Leo ('what Leo said') acknowledges his contribution respectfully, even while disagreeing.
Dimension 2: 'Fear sometimes LOOKS like selfishness' introduces a new, nuanced interpretation — this is new reasoning, not repetition.
Dimension 3: 'Does that change anyone's thinking?' is an open invitation for further discussion.
This response models all three dimensions of excellent collaborative discussion.

items.prompt:
A student has been listening carefully and notices that three classmates are all saying slightly different things that actually support one big idea. What is the best contribution she can make?
A) Pick the best of the three ideas and ignore the others
B) Synthesize: 'I think all three of your ideas connect — together they show that the main character changed because of three different challenges'
C) Tell the three students to agree with each other before continuing
items.answer: B) Synthesize: 'I think all three of your ideas connect — together they show that the main character changed because of three different challenges'

steps: Synthesis means combining multiple ideas into a larger connected understanding.
Option A discards valuable contributions unnecessarily.
Option C is directive and unhelpful.
Option B explicitly connects all three ideas and shows how they support a bigger point.
Synthesis is the most advanced form of building on others' talk.

items.prompt:
A student often has great ideas but rarely speaks in discussions because she is shy. Under the discussion rules, what is the best way for the GROUP to help?
A) Ignore it — discussions are only for confident students
B) Make her speak by putting her on the spot in front of everyone
C) Invite her gently: 'Sofia, we haven't heard from you — do you have a thought?' — and make the group a safe space where all ideas are welcomed
items.answer: C) Invite her gently: 'Sofia, we haven't heard from you — do you have a thought?' — and make the group a safe space where all ideas are welcomed

steps: Collaborative discussions require everyone's participation — including quieter students.
Putting someone on the spot forcefully can make shyness worse.
A gentle invitation ('do you have a thought?') shows care and creates a welcoming environment.
The group's responsibility includes making sure all voices are encouraged, not just the loudest ones.

items.prompt:
A student says something factually incorrect in a discussion (e.g., 'The sun revolves around the Earth'). How should a classmate respond while following discussion rules?
A) Laugh and move on
B) 'Actually, I think it is the other way around — the Earth revolves around the sun. I am not 100% sure, so maybe we can check, but can you tell me where you heard that?'
C) 'You are so wrong. Everyone knows that.'
items.answer: B) 'Actually, I think it is the other way around — the Earth revolves around the sun. I am not 100% sure, so maybe we can check, but can you tell me where you heard that?'

steps: Option A ignores the error — the group continues with false information.
Option C is disrespectful and shuts down the conversation.
Option B respectfully corrects the statement, acknowledges the student might not be 100% certain, and asks for clarification ('where did you hear that?').
This is respectful correction combined with intellectual humility and a request for further explanation.

items.prompt:
After a discussion ends, a student reflects: 'I talked a lot but I don't actually remember what anyone else said.' What does this tell you about her listening skills, and what should she do differently next time?
A) Nothing — talking more is always better in discussions
B) She was not listening to others carefully. Next time, she should take mental notes of what classmates say so she can link her comments to theirs
C) She needs to speak less, but listening skills are not part of discussion rules
items.answer: B) She was not listening to others carefully. Next time, she should take mental notes of what classmates say so she can link her comments to theirs

steps: Not remembering what others said indicates the student was focused on her own contributions, not listening.
Listening 'with care' is one of the core discussion rules.
Actively noting what classmates say allows you to link your comments to theirs — a key discussion skill.
Good discussion is a BALANCE of speaking and careful listening.

items.prompt:
A student asks: 'When I disagree with someone in a discussion, should I always say WHY I disagree, or is it okay to just say I disagree?'
A) Just saying 'I disagree' is enough — no reasons are needed
B) Explaining WHY you disagree is better because it advances the discussion and shows you have thought about the idea
C) You should never disagree in a classroom discussion
items.answer: B) Explaining WHY you disagree is better because it advances the discussion and shows you have thought about the idea

steps: Simply saying 'I disagree' does not add information to the discussion.
Explaining your reasoning ('I disagree because...') shows active engagement and gives others something to respond to.
Discussions that include reasons and evidence are more productive.
Respectful disagreement WITH reasoning is encouraged in collaborative discussions.

items.prompt:
A group of students is discussing a book. One student keeps bringing the discussion back to his personal experiences ('That happened to me...') without connecting them to the book. Is this good discussion behavior?
A) Yes — personal connections always improve discussions
B) It can be, but only if the personal connection is linked back to the text or topic under discussion
C) No — personal connections are never allowed in discussions
items.answer: B) It can be, but only if the personal connection is linked back to the text or topic under discussion

steps: Personal connections can enrich discussion when they illuminate the text.
Example: 'That happened to me too — and it made me feel just like the character probably felt.'
But if the student just talks about himself without linking to the book, the discussion loses focus.
The rule: stay on the topics and texts under discussion. Connections are good when they serve that goal.

items.prompt:
Evaluate this student's self-assessment after a discussion: 'I listened to my classmates, asked two questions when I was confused, added new information twice, and disagreed respectfully once while explaining my reasons.' Based on the discussion rules, how well did this student participate?
A) Poorly — they did too many things at once
B) Excellently — they demonstrated listening, clarifying, building, and respectful disagreement
C) Adequately — they should have only done one of those things
items.answer: B) Excellently — they demonstrated listening, clarifying, building, and respectful disagreement

steps: Listening carefully: check.
Asking questions when confused (asking for clarification): check.
Adding new information (building on others' talk): check.
Respectful disagreement with reasoning: check.
This student demonstrated all the key sub-skills of 2.SL.A.1 in a single discussion.
